items.prompt: The issues cursor encodes createdAt AND id. Why is the id needed?
items.answer: Rows with equal createdAt could be skipped without it
distractors: It lets the server jump straight to any numbered page
A bare createdAt cannot be base64url-encoded safely
It proves the client may read the team of that row
items.explanation: The keyset predicate is createdAt < c.createdAt OR (createdAt = c.createdAt AND id < c.id), matching the (createdAt desc, id desc) order. Without the id tie-breaker, rows with an equal createdAt after the page boundary would be lost.

items.prompt: decodeCursor gets a cursor whose decoded text has no "|" in it. What does it return?
items.answer: null, so the list query runs with no keyset filter
distractors: It throws, and the route answers 400 with BAD_FILTER
A cursor whose id is set to an empty string instead
A cursor with createdAt holding the whole decoded text
items.explanation: split("|") yields a single element, so id is undefined and the guard `if (!createdAt || !id) return null` fires. With a null cursor the route adds no keyset predicate and returns the first page.

items.prompt: What does keyBetween("a", "b") return?
items.answer: The two-character key "aV"
distractors: The two-character key "ab"
The two-character key "a5"
The one-character key "V"
items.explanation: "a" (index 36) and "b" (37) are adjacent, so the loop copies "a" and goes one level deeper. There lo is padded with 0 and hi with 62, so mid = 31, which is "V". "aV" sorts after "a" and before "b".

items.prompt: What is planted flaw #2 in fractional indexing, and when is it harvested?
items.answer: Keys grow longer on same-slot inserts; Sprint 12 rebalances
distractors: Two clients can mint one key; Sprint 07 adds a lock around moves
Keys lose precision after ~50 inserts; Sprint 12 swaps in floats
Lowercase keys sort wrongly; Sprint 12 replaces the alphabet
items.explanation: Repeated inserts between the same neighbours make keys longer each time. evenKeys (S12) reassigns a column to evenly spaced short keys. Precision loss is the float alternative the ADR rejected; the alphabet is already in ascending ASCII order.

items.prompt: recordMutation calls fanout.publish only after its transaction commits. Why?
items.answer: Publishing first could show clients a write that rolls back
distractors: Publishing inside it would deadlock the workspace seq update
The fanout needs the commit timestamp to put deltas in order
Clients drop any delta that arrives before its row is indexed
items.explanation: The comment says it directly: announcing an uncommitted mutation would let clients see state that then rolls back. Order comes from the seq allocated inside the transaction, not from a timestamp.

items.prompt: A client misses one fanout delta while its socket is down. How does it get the change?
items.answer: It replays the log from its lastSeq when it reconnects
distractors: The server resends that delta until the client acks it
It does not; the change stays missing until the next edit
It asks the other clients in the workspace to send it
items.explanation: The log is truth and the fanout is a hint: each mutation is a durable row with a monotonic per-workspace seq, and a client catches up from its lastSeq. Nothing in the fanout retries or relays between clients.

items.prompt: In the overlay store, how is a rejected optimistic edit rolled back?
items.answer: Its pending mutation is dropped; committed was never changed
distractors: committed is restored from an undo copy taken before the edit
The server sends an inverse delta that cancels out the edit
The whole store is reloaded from IndexedDB after the failure
items.explanation: Optimistic edits live only in `pending`; the view is materialize(committed, pending). Removing the pending entry removes the edit from the view, with no undo logic.

items.prompt: A server delta arrives whose mutationId matches a pending entry. What happens to that entry?
items.answer: It is acked: it leaves pending, and committed holds the value
distractors: It stays, and materialize keeps showing the optimistic one
It is ignored, since the edit is already visible on the screen
It is sent again so the server can confirm the ack it received
items.explanation: applyServerDelta writes the value into committed and ackMutation filters the matching mutationId out of pending, so the server's value now shows from committed.

items.prompt: A client lost the ack and resends a create with the same mutationId. What does the API return?
items.answer: The issue first created for that mutationId, not a second one
distractors: 409 Conflict, telling the client to drop its pending create
A second issue, which the client is then expected to delete
400, as a given mutationId may only ever be submitted once
items.explanation: The create handler looks up mutationLog by workspaceId + mutationId; if it was seen, it loads that entity and returns it. That is the exactly-once-in-effect rule.

items.prompt: What does Tracer store in Postgres for a signed-in session?
items.answer: A SHA-256 hash of the cookie token, with userId and expiresAt
distractors: The raw cookie token, so the lookup is one plain equality check
A signed JWT copy, so a token can be checked without the cookie
The user's OAuth access token, refreshed on every API request
items.explanation: createSession stores tokenHash: hashToken(token) and returns the raw token for the cookie; getUserByToken hashes the cookie value and looks it up. Revocation is deleting the row.

items.prompt: Why does presence ("Ada is viewing ENG") stay out of the mutation log?
items.answer: It is high-churn and worthless a moment later, so it would only bloat it
distractors: The log only accepts entities that have a database row and a team id
Presence must be encrypted, but the log keeps its patches as plain JSON
It has to reach other workspaces, which the log does not fan out to
items.explanation: Presence is a heartbeat every few seconds per viewer; logging it would add millions of rows an hour and slow every bootstrap. Durability is a choice per state kind.

items.prompt: The S15 drill killed pub/sub mid-collaboration. What did the team treat as the real incident?
items.answer: The API looked healthy while fanout was dead, so no page fired
distractors: Clients lost unsent edits, as the pub/sub connection dropped
The durable log fell behind and needed a manual replay to recover
Reconnecting clients stampeded and took the database offline
items.explanation: Clients kept working from their overlay and caught up from lastSeq, so nothing was lost. The gap was observability: no alert fired. The fix is a fanout-liveness alert plus reconnect backoff with jitter.

items.front: Routing rule for any new collaborative state (ADR-0008)
items.back: Ask: does it need to be correct across devices and survive a reload? Yes -> the mutation log (like comments). No -> an ephemeral channel (like presence on the in-process presenceBus).
Inside one transaction it increments workspace.mutationSeq and writes the mutationLog row with that seq. Atomic per workspace, so the log has a total order; the fanout publish happens after commit.

Copy committed, then apply each pending mutation in order (delete removes, create/update writes its value). Rollback = drop a pending entry; rebase happens on every render because the overlay is re-applied over new committed truth.
Cookie tracer_session: httpOnly, sameSite lax, secure only in production, path /, maxAge 30 days. It carries a random token; only its SHA-256 hash is stored.

items.prompt: ADR-0001 rejected Next.js for Tracer's web shell. Apart from near-zero SEO value behind auth, what conflict with server rendering did it name?
items.answer: A server render would split-brain against the local-first store
distractors: File-based routing would clash with the keyboard shortcut registry
Server-rendered HTML would cache one team's issues for another team
SSR would open a second WebSocket per tab beside the sync engine
items.explanation: ADR-0001 lines 19-23: Next.js was rejected because an auth-gated tool gets almost no SEO benefit, and SSR introduces a server-render vs. local-state "split-brain" that fights the local-first store built in S07; the WebSocket/local-first story is simpler in a pure SPA. The ADR names no routing, HTML-caching or extra-socket problem.

items.prompt: ADR-0001 names one condition for revisiting the Vite SPA decision. What is it, and how does the ADR suggest handling it?
items.answer: A public SEO surface, built as a separate Next.js app
distractors: Slow first loads, fixed by moving this app to Next.js
A mobile client, built by porting this app to native
Offline bugs, fixed by adding SSR to this same app
items.explanation: ADR-0001 lines 29-30: revisit if a public, SEO-relevant surface (a marketing site or shared public boards) is added, and that could live in a separate Next.js app rather than reshaping this one. Load speed, a mobile client and offline bugs are not the named trigger, and the ADR explicitly avoids reshaping the existing app.

items.prompt: How does ADR-0002 describe the Sprint 1-5 REST + TanStack Query architecture, and why does it name the sync endgame on day one?
items.answer: As a planned throwaway; the endgame shaped the SPA and per-field mutations
distractors: As a lasting fallback; the endgame kept a REST mode alive for offline users
As a demo-only build; the endgame let the team skip tests on the REST code
As a shared base layer; the endgame let both data layers ship side by side
items.explanation: ADR-0002 lines 14-21: the classic architecture is a deliberate, planned throwaway whose replacement is the core lesson, and the endgame is named so every early decision is made with it in view, e.g. choosing a SPA and per-field mutation granularity because the sync engine will need them. Lines 30-31 add that the TanStack Query layer is intentionally deleted in S06-07, so it is neither kept nor shipped alongside.

items.prompt: ADR-0002's Revisit line says "never". What reason does it give?
items.answer: It is a teaching decision that no scale could overturn
distractors: Its sync engine was load-tested past any target scale
Deleting the REST layer makes it impossible to reverse
The Meridian course fixed the roadmap for every course
items.explanation: ADR-0002 lines 34-35: "Revisit: never — this is a pedagogical decision, not a technical one that scale could overturn." No load test is cited, deleting the classic layer is described as a feature rather than the reason, and Meridian is only mentioned as precedent elsewhere.

items.prompt: Tracer's filter AST (ADR-0009) compiles to a client evaluator and a server Prisma where. What stops user input from becoming a raw column name?
items.answer: The field set is a closed enum validated by zod
distractors: compileFilter escapes each field name before use
Only filters saved as a view reach the server side
Prisma refuses a where clause on unindexed columns
items.explanation: ADR-0009 lines 19-20: the field set is a closed enum, validated by zod, so user input can never become a raw column name; saved views store the AST as data. Safety comes from that closed set, not from escaping names, from a saved-view-only rule, or from any Prisma index check.

items.prompt: Tracer's command palette (ADR-0010) finds both actions and issues. Where does each kind of result come from?
items.answer: Commands ranked locally; issues from a debounced server search
distractors: Both from the local store, with a server search only when offline
Commands from the server; issues fuzzy-ranked from IndexedDB
Both from one server index that each client caches per team
items.explanation: ADR-0010 lines 13-16: two systems are merged so the user never sees the seam. Commands are fuzzy-ranked locally and instantly, boosted by frecency; issues come from a debounced server search across the user's teams, covering the long tail the local store has not loaded. A server search cannot run offline, and there is no single shared index.

items.prompt: ADR-0010 keeps a hand-rolled fuzzy matcher instead of Fuse.js or minisearch. What trigger does it name for adopting a library?
items.answer: Multi-field weighting across entity types past ~200 lines
distractors: The matcher's share of the bundle passing about 20 kB
User ranking complaints passing a few per sprint
The issues per team passing what the client loaded
items.explanation: ADR-0010 lines 21-23: the library was rejected because the matcher is about 80 lines, adds zero bundle and is fully tunable; the named trigger to adopt one is multi-field weighting across entity types past roughly 200 lines. Bundle size, complaint counts and the unloaded long tail are not the trigger; the long tail is what the server search covers.

items.prompt: Per ADR-0010's consequences, why must the server issue search be permission-scoped, and where does frecency live?
items.answer: Unscoped search exfiltrates data; frecency stays client-side
distractors: Unscoped search is too slow; frecency is shared on the server
Unscoped search breaks caching; frecency is stored per team
Unscoped search skews ranking; frecency is global in Redis
items.explanation: ADR-0010 lines 30-32: frecency lives client-side because it is your own muscle memory, not shared state, and the server search is permission-scoped (guests only search their teams) because a search index that forgets scoping is a data-exfiltration API. Speed, caching and ranking are not the stated reasons, and frecency is neither shared, per-team nor in Redis.

items.prompt: How does ADR-0011 keep the `?` shortcut-help overlay from falling out of date as bindings are added?
items.answer: It reads the same registry that dispatches the keys
distractors: CI diffs it against a hand-kept cheatsheet document
Each binding's author adds a line to the help file
It is rebuilt from the keyboard tests on every build
items.explanation: ADR-0011 lines 23-25: the overlay reads useRegistry().list(), the same registry that dispatches keys, so behavior and documentation share one source and cannot drift; adding a shortcut makes it appear in help for free. A hand-maintained cheatsheet is the rejected alternative (lines 38-39), and no tests or authored help lines are involved.

items.prompt: ADR-0011 announces live collaborative changes through a single live region. Which politeness level did it pick, and what does that still not guarantee?
items.answer: Polite; a silent DOM change still needs an explicit show()
distractors: Polite; every DOM mutation is then announced automatically
Assertive; polite regions are skipped by most screen readers
Assertive; a toast queued while typing is still dropped later
items.explanation: ADR-0011 lines 40-41 reject aria-live="assertive" because it interrupts on every teammate keystroke; collaborative changes are polite by nature. Lines 51-52: announcements are only as good as the events reaching the toast bus, so a component that mutates the DOM silently still needs to show() something, a review checklist item rather than a guarantee. Nothing is announced automatically.

items.prompt: In ADR-0011's three-tier theme cascade, which tier wins, and why was inline theming per component rejected?
items.answer: [data-theme] wins; inline styles couple color to components
distractors: :root wins; inline styles would ignore the OS preference query
prefers-color-scheme wins; inline styles slow the first paint
[data-theme] wins; inline styles would need a library like Radix
items.explanation: ADR-0011 lines 33-35: :root (dark default), then @media (prefers-color-scheme) to follow the OS when unset, then [data-theme], where an explicit choice wins; a swap is one attribute flip on <html>. Lines 45-46: JS-driven inline theming couples color to components and defeats the single-flip swap. Radix is a separate rejected alternative about accessible components, not theming.

items.prompt: Sprint 13's P1 finding: a guest scoped to Team A could read Team B's issue changes from raw WebSocket frames. What did the fix change?
items.answer: Deltas carry teamId; canSeeDelta gates live and backlog paths
distractors: The gateway now rechecks workspace membership on each frame
Guests open a separate socket for each team they are granted
The live path is filtered, while backlog is served over REST
items.explanation: Sprint 13 audit lines 10 and 20-22: the gateway had checked workspace membership and then forwarded every team's deltas. The fix makes every delta carry the teamId it changed, and canSeeDelta(membership, teamId) gates forwarding on both the live fanout path and the backlog stream. Workspace membership was the coarse check that leaked, and the backlog path is filtered too.

items.back: Foundation S01-S05: monorepo, auth, RBAC, issues CRUD, keyboard UI, canned views (build the boring spine well). The turn S06-S07: mutation log + WS gateway, offline overlay store (the log is truth, the network is a hint). Product depth S08-S11: ordering, undo/redo, comments, presence, saved filters (features are cheap on a correct spine). Scale & safety S12-S13: harvest the planted debt. Finish S14-S15: accessibility, observability, ops, incident drill, release.

items.front: Tracer's flaw ledger: how planted flaws were handled
items.back: Five flaws were planted on purpose and kept in an author-private ledger until the retrospective. Rule: never fix a planted flaw silently; every harvesting commit quoted the ledger row and flipped its status. Separate in-PR arcs were planted and fixed inside one PR to model tight debugging loops (e.g. S03's identifier-counter race fixed with SELECT FOR UPDATE). Why plant at all: you feel why a pattern exists only after living without it.

items.front: The spine dividend: what the expensive foundations paid for later
items.back: Mutation log (S06): undo/redo (S08) as inverse mutations, comments (S08) as just another synced entity. Overlay store + reconnect (S07): deploys made free by drain-as-reconnect, and the client joining distributed tracing (S15). Authz spine as pure functions (S02): reused verbatim on the WebSocket in S13, one rule for every transport. Each plumbing sprint bought a later feature at a discount.

items.front: Sprint 12 perf audit: the method, and findings P2-P4
items.back: Method: measure, rank by user impact, fix one thing per change, prove it with a before/after number; docs/latency-budget.md is the contract. P2 (severity P2): issue list/board renders every row, and a 10k-issue seed janks. P3 (severity P3): each mutation fans out its own delta frame, so bulk ops send N frames. P4 (severity P3): presence heartbeats every viewer unbatched (partly done with a 5 s heartbeat).

items.front: ADR-0011's three small platform primitives for keyboard users
items.back: A .skip-link that stays off-screen until focused (satisfies WCAG 2.4.1); :focus-visible outlines so the keyboard caret is obvious; and prefers-reduced-motion to disable non-essential transitions.

Subsequence matching with bonuses for consecutive runs, word boundaries and camelCase humps, plus a mild penalty for length. The ADR (and the file's own comment) call it about 80 lines; the pinned fuzzy.ts is 48. Ranking bugs count as regressions and are pinned with fixtures (the boundary/consecutive tests).

items.front: Tracer v2 ideas from the retrospective
items.back: GitHub integration (two-way issue sync: reconciliation, webhooks, their authz meeting ours); a mobile client sharing @tracer/shared; a text CRDT for collaborative comment/description editing, where the mutation-log model meets its limits; real infra: Redis-backed fanout (revisit ADR-0012's trigger), OTel + a tracing backend, load testing at 10k concurrent.

items.prompt: ADR-0009 says an equivalence test keeps the client evaluate and the server compileFilter from drifting. What does the pinned test suite actually cover?
items.answer: Only the client evaluate; nothing tests compileFilter
distractors: Both, through fixtures that the api tests also import
Only compileFilter, through the saved-views route test
Both, through an e2e spec that compares two filters
items.explanation: packages/shared/src/filter.test.ts imports only evaluate (line 2), and its two tests call evaluate alone. compileFilter (apps/api/src/lib/filter-compile.ts:10), which issues.ts:222 uses to build the Prisma where, appears in no test file: the api tests cover auth, fanout, pagination and the server, and e2e/ holds only keyboard.spec.ts. So the guard ADR-0009 lines 30-31 describe is not in the tree, and a filterable field added to one evaluator but not the other would fail nothing. There is no shared fixture, saved-views route test or e2e filter spec.

items.prompt: In the delivered web client, two updates to one issue (seq 6, then seq 7) reach the open socket in the order 7, then 6. What does useTeamIssues leave in committed for that issue?
items.answer: Seq 6's value, as each delta is applied when it arrives
distractors: Seq 7's value, as deltas are sorted by seq before applying
Seq 7's value, as a delta older than lastSeq is skipped
Neither: the out-of-order delta forces a full re-bootstrap
items.explanation: useTeamIssues.ts lines 67-85 handle every live delta the moment it arrives: lastSeqRef keeps the maximum seq, and applyServerDelta(s.committed, ...) writes the delta's value. applyServerDelta (store.ts lines 36-45) overwrites the entity without comparing seq, so the late seq-6 value replaces seq 7's. reduceDeltas (store.ts lines 47-53) does sort by seq, but only store.test.ts calls it, so the Sprint 13 audit's order-independence holds for that reducer, not for this live path. Nothing skips older deltas or triggers a re-bootstrap.
